 Latest news The SSA’s latest cost-of-living adjustment will change benefits, and expand the income subject to Social Security tax next year.
 Getty Images Social Security Goodbye to the $184,500 maximum tax income limit in 2027: Updated maximum amount of taxable earnings for Social Security
 Calum Roche twitter Joseph McMahon twitter Greg Heilman Update: Oct 22nd, 2026 10:03 EDT Share Make us preferred on Google The Social Security Administration (SSA) announced the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for beneficiaries on 14 October 2026. This annual boost to the amount Social Security sent to recipients each month is designed to maintain the purchasing power of benefits as prices rise from one year to the next.
 The COLA doesn’t just affect benefit checks – it also influences how much of a worker’s income is subject to Social Security taxes. 
 Although the 12.4 percent tax on wages remains in place, the maximum income that can be taxed will rise again in 2027. The Social Security tax is split evenly between workers and employers, each paying 6.2 percent of the employee’s earnings. That rate has stayed the same since 1990, but the maximum taxable earnings limit continues to increase year by year. 
 How much is the maximum amount of earnings to be taxed in 2027?
 The maximum amount of income subject to Social Security tax in 2027 is $192,300, up from $184,500 in 2026.  Income above this threshold will not be taxed for Social Security purposes.
 This change means that higher earners will contribute more toward the program in 2027. Here’s how the taxable maximum has evolved over the past decade: 
 Year Amount 
 2017 $127,200 
 2018 $128,400 
 2019 $132,900 
 2020 $137,700 
 2021 $142,800 
 2022 $147,000 
 2023 $160,200 
 2024 $168,600 
 2025 $176,100 
 2026 $184,500 
 2027 $192,300 
 2027 COLA: Benefits to rise by 3.6%
 Based on the increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI-W) from the third quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026, Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment in 2027. 
 That means the average retiree’s monthly payment will go from $2,095 to $2,170 – a modest but meaningful bump designed to keep pace with inflation.
 Here’s a look at how average payments will change:
 Category 2026 2027 
 All Retired Workers $2,095 $2,170 
 Aged Couple, Both Receiving Benefits $3,238 $3,355 
 Widowed Mother and Two Children $3,932 $4,074 
 Aged Widow(er) Alone $1,936 $2,005 
 All Disabled Workers $1,642 $1,701 
 Other key Social Security changes for 2026
 The SSA has also announced several other important updates for next year:
 Category 2026 2027 
 Quarter of Coverage $1,890 $1,970 
 Retirement Earnings Test (Under full retirement age) $24,480/yr. ($2,040/mo.) $25,560/yr. ($2,130/mo.) 
 Earnings Limit (Year you reach full retirement age) $65,160/yr. ($5,430/mo.) $67,920/yr. ($5,660/mo.) 
 Disability Threshold (Non-Blind) $1,690/mo. $1,770/mo. 
 Disability Threshold (Blind) $2,830/mo. $2,950/mo. 
 Trial Work Period $1,210/mo. $1,270/mo. 
 Maximum Benefit at Full Retirement Age $4,152/mo. $4,188/mo. 
 SSI Payment Standard (Individual) $994/mo. $1,029/mo. 
 SSI Payment Standard (Couple) $1,491/mo. $1,544/mo. 
 The resource limits for SSI – $2,000 for individuals and $3,000 for couples – will remain unchanged in 2027.
 Social Security tax rates remain the same
 The overall tax rate for 2027 will not change:
 Employees: 7.65% (6.2% for Social Security + 1.45% for Medicare) 
 Self-employed workers: 15.3% total 
 High earners making over $200,000 (or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly) will continue to pay an additional 0.9% Medicare surtax , as in previous years.
 What if you have multiple jobs?
 For workers with more than one employer in a year, each employer must withhold Social Security taxes up to the maximum limit. If your combined wages across jobs exceed $192,300, you may end up paying more than the maximum amount. In that case, you can claim a refund for the excess Social Security tax withheld when filing your federal tax return with the IRS.
